podcast.body: The music video for this song from 1982 was noted for being slicker, glossier, and more expensive than earlier low-tech productions. Its sophisticated visual style significantly contributed to changing the very sound of new wave from its powerpop and post-punk roots to the emerging synthpop genre, marking a "changing of the guard" moment in the music industry. "By 1982, videos like The Human Leagues don't you want me, were not only Slicker, Glossier, and more expensive. They were changing the very sound of new wave from Powerpop and Postpunk to Synthpop."

podcast.body: This 1980s new wave hit is an example of a song/band influenced by Donna Summer's "I Feel Love," with music journalist Simon Reynolds suggesting "the 1980s began with I Feel Love." "The music journalist Simon Reynolds said that the 1980s began with I Feel Love and when you consider the new wave music that was so prevalent in that era and you can hear it starting in I Feel Love, it's really hard to argue with him on that."

This 1981 song by The Human League achieved significant popularity and became a major hit on MTV, showcasing the band's distinctive technopop sound and visual appeal. "The human league with Don't You Want Me From 1981."

podcast.body: This song, a romantic melodrama brought to life by Oakey and Sulley, was the last track and fourth single from the *Dare* album. Oakey initially thought it was "filler" and "NAF" and tried to dissuade his label, Virgin, from releasing it as a 45. However, Virgin commissioned their most expensive music video to date—a "meta-film noir" loosely based on *A Star Is Born*, making it the "highest gloss clip on MTV at the time." It reached UK number one in December 1981 (Christmas number one) and US number one in July 1982, after an 18-week climb, becoming their biggest hit on both sides of the Atlantic. "Oki thought the song was filler, he called it NAF, and he tried to dissuade his label, Virgin, from putting it out as a 45."
